Putting people first in design: P&T's Mark Ong on listening and making each project count
article:
Early in Mark Ong’s career in architecture and urban design, he tended to focus more on a project's look and feel, particular approaches and buzzwords such as creating "iconic" buildings.

"When you first start out and you're young, you may still be very, very idealistic and have certain fixations or programming in your mind about what you want architecture to be," says Ong, Singapore-based group director at international architectural engineering practice P&T Consultants.

But as he worked on more projects, Ong began paying more attention to the many considerations and perspectives that feed into a development.

One skill he came to appreciate more was listening — to clients, authorities and other stakeholders involved in each project.

"You have to listen, not just in meetings but also in the briefs that clients write for you, in the speeches made in the media, and in the guidelines," he says.

"Read between the lines and discern the subtleties. What's the vision behind their ideas for the city, a particular neighbourhood, and down to a specific site?"

Over time, his thinking has evolved towards a more human-centred approach that considers how spaces connect and the feelings and environments they create for people moving through them.

"I find those to be far more important now, and it's those things that eventually determine the look and feel of things, rather than a preconceived idea of a look and feel."

This focus on people is also part of P&T's thinking, encompassing buyers, residents and other end-users, developers, the authorities and policymakers.

Each will bring their own needs and inputs to a project, which P&T then distils and brings together in the final design.

Starting with people and context

An ongoing mixed-use project currently on P&T’s drawing board illustrates how several groups can use and share a development in their own ways.

Situated near the city centre and a river, this project will combine residential, commercial and hospitality uses.

People will use the development for varying purposes and lengths of time — from residents who buy and live in the apartments for the long term, to tourists and business travellers staying for shorter periods, as well as customers visiting the commercial spaces.

"We're thinking about how to weave these elements together to give everybody their own place so they won't intrude on each other, while also finding that sweet spot where they can be together to enjoy the site," Ong says.

Finding that balance starts with what he calls "context", which is P&T's typical starting point with any new project.

The firm looks at the physical conditions of the site — its topography and shape, what surrounds it and the possible connections that can be created — while also understanding the regulatory requirements and what the client envisions for the project.

"Some clients already have very crystallised notions and have decided what they want to do. Others leave things more open-ended and seek our insights," Ong notes.

With the latter, conversations between P&T and the client help determine the direction. "The design that comes out is generally an outcome of that dialogue," he adds.

Working with a site's character

The physical quirks of a site may also provide opportunities to create some of a development's most distinctive spaces.

At the Bartley Residences condo along Lorong How Sun, completed in 2015, the team faced three challenges with the site.

Ong recalls it had an "awkward" irregular shape, a natural topography with several storeys of elevation difference from one end to the other, and a large, ancient Bodhi tree that was to be preserved. Estimated to be around 140 years old as of 2026, the tree rises over 30m tall and has an 8.5m girth.

"We crafted the site plan such that we could preserve this tree," Ong says.

As a result, P&T created two key open spaces, each with its own centrepiece: the swimming pool in one and the towering Bodhi tree in the other.

This is unlike many condos, where the pool usually dominates the main communal area.

The site's topography also influenced the design of the arrival area at Bartley Residences. From the welcome drop-off pavilion, residents can look down towards the pool from an elevation that Ong likens to being "perched on a small cliff, which gives a little bit of drama to the space".

"That's an example of how the circumstances of a site can create a point of interest," he says.

Signature features born from creative solutions

At Hougang Capeview , an HDB project next to Serangoon River, the firm had another unusual site to work with.

Besides giving as many homes as possible views towards the river, the team was tasked with adding a spatial corridor through the development that would open to views towards the waterfront.

"To establish that axis, we created a small retail street within the site and it culminated in a viewing deck that overlooked the river," Ong says. "It's an interesting HDB project, with this distinct feature."

And at The Continuum , an upcoming condo in District 15, P&T designed a single development across two separate plots sitting on either side of Thiam Siew Avenue.

To link the two halves, the team sought the authorities' approval to introduce a private overhead pedestrian bridge across the road.

Weaving through the landscaping and elevated over the condo's pools, the sky bridge is designed to be a new landmark in the neighbourhood.

This connection also allowed the team to give each plot its own character. "You can create a distinct environment on each side. It's two different worlds, and connecting them lets residents enjoy both worlds," Ong says.

In addition, the project conserves one of the original pre-war bungalows from the landed housing estate that previously occupied the site, converting it into a clubhouse named Thiam Siew House.

"That's another example of turning the unusual circumstances of a project into a signature talking point," Ong adds.

Building on lessons from each project

While many projects may call for innovative ways of tackling design challenges, he hesitates to describe P&T's approach to architecture as "experimentation" — particularly when designing homes that buyers are often purchasing with their life savings.

"We do not take that responsibility lightly. So, we take careful steps [with new ideas] and are very, very considerate about things that we can try out," Ong shares.

When a solution shows promise on one project, the firm may take it further in other developments and build on what has worked well before.

"We want to make sure that when a resident buys a home, they benefit from a combination of our best learnings at that point in time," he adds.

Ong brings a similar perspective to the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards 2026 as a judge in the design and architecture specialisation.

Besides reviewing each project's submission to understand what it sets out to achieve, the judging process gives him the opportunity to see how closely the completed developments or showflats align with that intent.

Among the residential entries for this year's awards, UpperHouse At Orchard Boulevard was one of the uncompleted projects that impressed Ong, while Tembusu Grand caught his attention during visits to the completed developments.

"The architectural expression of UpperHouse captures the distinctive qualities of the layout, of what’s inside the building, quite elegantly. It's refreshing," Ong says.

For Tembusu Grand, he reckons the response to the site was "well done", from the arrival experience and walking the grounds through the common areas, to the "very cleverly concealed" back-of-house spaces such as the car park.

"There's not a lot of gymnastics, no outlandish forms. Everything just works well," he says of the condo on Jalan Tembusu.

Seeing the work of other teams through the judging process also ties into his belief that designers ought to keep raising the bar with each project.

"I would encourage all designers to have that mindset of always seeking to make their latest project their best, by taking on board all of the learnings from the past," Ong says.

"Each new project should embody how far you have evolved."

title: Singapore’s Hidden Cash Kings: Top 3 Debt-Free Stocks for Reliable Dividends
article:
If you have gone to your local
kopitiam
and ordered
a cup of
kopi
lately, you already know the story – cash simply doesn’t stretch as far or earn as much as it did a year ago.
HRnetGroup Limited
(SGX: CHZ),
Credit Bureau Asia Limited
(SGX: TCU) and
VICOM Ltd
(SGX: WJP) all reported lower interest income for the first half of 2026 (1H2026).
Yet, all three still managed to raise their interim dividends.
How? None of them carry bank borrowings, excluding lease liabilities.
That pristine net-cash position gives each board plenty of elbow room to reward shareholders.
But a rising payout still needs an underlying business that can actually afford it.
Free cash flow is the ultimate lifeblood of any payout, so let’s check each company’s cash flow against its latest

Can VICOM keep raising its dividend as its ERP 2.0 work winds down?
VICOM, a subsidiary of
ComfortDelGro Corporation
(SGX: C52), runs vehicle inspection and non-vehicle testing services.
It ended June 2026 with S$53 million in cash and zero bank borrowings, against lease liabilities of S$33.3 million.
Of the trio, VICOM makes the most straightforward dividend case.
Its interim dividend rose 27.4% year on year (YoY) to S$0.0395 per share.
Earnings per share (EPS) climbed from S$0.0439 to S$0.0561.
Simply put, the dividend grew in step with profit.
Revenue rose 6.4% to S$74.3 million, while operating costs fell 1.2% as subcontractor fees for the ERP 2.0 On-Board Unit (OBU) project dropped 44.2%.
Interest income also halved to S$0.4 million.
Profit attributable to shareholders climbed 28% to S$19.9 million.
The cash followed the profit, too.
Operating cash flow rose 65.1% to S$31.8 million – easily covering S$17.2 million of capital expenditure.
Free cash flow more than doubled to S$14.7 million, up from S$6 million previously.
Management expects a softer second half.
It sees steady demand from electronics and precision engineering, but more uncertainty in oil & gas because of the Middle East conflict.
OBU installations will taper off before the project ends in December 2026.

This Unassuming Singapore Stock Could Fund Your Retirement Income
How far can HRnetGroup’s cash carry its dividend through a hiring slowdown?
HRnetGroup runs recruitment and staffing businesses across 19 Asian cities.
As at 30 June 2026, it held S$332.1 million in cash, treasury bills and gold, with no borrowings.
No other company on this list comes close to that war chest.
With that backing, the board bumped up the interim dividend by 10% YoY to S$0.022 per share.
The core business did its job.
Revenue slipped just 1.1% to S$292.2 million (remaining flat in constant-currency terms), while gross profit grew 1.5% to S$62.1 million.
Operating expenses fell 1.9%, which lifted operating profit by 9.4% to S$20.1 million.
Other income moved the other way.
It fell 65.5% to S$5.4 million as government subsidies and interest income shrank, and HRnetGroup’s investments swung to a fair value loss.
Free cash flow dropped 34.3% to S$17.4 million, down from S$26.5 million a year earlier.
Management expects cyclical headwinds to persist, though the team is actively building recurring income through platforms like Octomate, YesPay! and Doudou.
This is where the cash buffer matters.
It gives the board room to keep paying through a downturn, though free cash flow is the key metric we’ll want to watch closely next time.
Related articles:
3 Cash-Rich SGX Dividend Stocks With Over 4% Yield
Beyond STI: 3 Singapore Dividend Stocks Offering Steady Passive Income
Why is Credit Bureau Asia’s dividend growing faster than its profit?
Credit Bureau Asia (CBA) supplies credit and risk information in Singapore, Malaysia, Cambodia and Myanmar.
As at 30 June 2026, it held S$49.6 million in cash and bank balances, plus S$2.2 million in financial assets.
It carries zero bank debt, with lease liabilities standing at S$4.7 million.
Its cash balance looks lower than a year ago, but for good reason: CBA completed a capital reduction on 26 June 2026, returning S$0.09 per share (roughly S$20.7 million) to shareholders.
That was a one-off capital return, completely separate from the ordinary dividend.
Its ordinary interim dividend rose 10% to S$0.022 per share (up from S$0.02), paid out on 28 August 2026.
Revenue rose 2.7% YoY to S$31 million, and free cash flow grew 4.6% to S$13.3 million.
Group profit also rose 3.6% to S$13.3 million.
Shareholders saw much less of that growth.
Profit attributable to them grew just 1.5% to S$5.5 million.
Where did the rest go? CBA runs its credit bureaux for financial institutions through joint ventures, and minority partners take a large share of the profit.
As a result, the dividend is currently growing faster than the net profit that actually belongs to equity holders.
Looking ahead, management sees Cambodia recovering, Myanmar improving, and remains cautiously optimistic about the rest of FY2026.
Related articles:
3 Debt-Free SGX Stocks Paying More Than Your CPF OA
Beyond Blue Chips: 3 Cash-Rich SGX Stocks Boosting Dividends 10%+
Get Smart: Check what the cash is worth to you
A net-cash figure gives you a great snapshot of what a company holds today, but it won’t tell you how comfortable next year’s
dividend
will feel.
Start with lease liabilities.
VICOM’s S$33.3 million in leases takes a far bigger bite out of its S$53 million cash pool than CBA’s S$4.7 million does relative to its stash.
Next, make sure you compare dividend payouts against the profit and cash flow that belong specifically to shareholders, rather than looking at group totals alone – CBA shows how group numbers can easily flatter the headline picture.
With interest income shrinking across the board, ask yourself one simple question every earnings season: Can the business alone cover your dividend?
For VICOM, this half, the answer is a clear yes.
Its EPS of S$0.0561 sits well above the S$0.0395 interim dividend.
For HRnetGroup and CBA, you’ll need the next set of results to answer with confidence.

title: Crypto elite gather in Singapore as bitcoin’s rally buoys bulls
article:
(Oct 6): Crypto’s movers and shakers are gathering in Singapore for one of their biggest conferences of the year as a bitcoin-led rally revives hopes that a new bull market is taking shape.

About 25,000 people are expected to converge on the city-state’s iconic Marina Bay Sands this week for Token2049. More than 500 exhibitors and 300 speakers are slated for the Oct 7-8 event, including Hyperliquid chief executive officer Jeff Yan, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan and World Liberty Financial co-founder Eric Trump.

Bitcoin’s rally from US$58,000 ($74,221) at the end of June to roughly US$86,000 today has spurred talk that the crypto winter is thawing, though the market has yet to regain the momentum and confidence of earlier bull cycles. Token2049 may offer insights into what crypto’s founders, builders, investors and financial institutions are betting on next.

“I’ve been one of the few attending Token2049 since the first one in 2018; looking back highlights just how far this asset class has matured,” said Dovey Wan, founding partner of crypto investment firm Primitive Ventures. “Through every boom and bust, staying in the game with those who built from day one is what truly matters.”

The industry has weathered a prolonged slump since October last year, when bitcoin plunged from its record high above US$126,000. But a 43% advance in the three months through September gave the largest cryptocurrency its strongest quarter since the final three months of 2024, when crypto-friendly US President Donald Trump won reelection.

One of the first keynote addresses of the conference is titled “Crypto Spring Turning Into Full Blown Bull Market” from BitMine chairman Tom Lee.

Still, bitcoin has struggled to break above US$87,000 as rising Treasury yields weigh on speculative assets.

See also: Singapore's crypto growth puts focus on cross-border payments: Chainalysis

The mood is better than it was in June, but it’s “definitely not euphoria”, said Haseeb Qureshi, managing partner at crypto-focused venture capital firm Dragonfly.

The market has absorbed setbacks such as the US Senate’s failure to advance the Clarity Act, while growing institutional participation and the expansion of stablecoin use have helped support confidence, he said.

One major theme at the conference will be how parts of traditional finance are moving onto blockchain networks, essentially putting assets and financial transactions on technology originally developed for cryptocurrencies. Tokenised assets, stablecoins and around-the-clock trading are increasingly bringing the two worlds closer together.

The value of tokenised real-world assets such as bonds, commodities and equities has surged, reaching more than US$38 billion at the end of September, according to RWA.xyz, whose tally excludes stablecoins.

The speaker lineup reflects that growing convergence, with crypto-native executives appearing alongside traditional financial industry leaders including Nasdaq chair and CEO Adena Friedman and Franklin Templeton CEO Jenny Johnson.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Eric Trump, the US president’s second son and executive vice president of the Trump Organization, will speak on “The Future of Finance, Built in America”.

Other big-name speakers include Ethereum co-founder Joseph Lubin, Binance co-CEO Richard Teng and crypto billionaire Justin Sun, an early investor in the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial who is now embroiled in a dispute with it.

Reigning Formula One champion Lando Norris, in town for this week’s Singapore Grand Prix, is also speaking at a session titled “The Drive to Win”.

Notably absent from this year’s lineup are Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino and Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev, who were both key speakers in 2025.

Artificial intelligence will be another major thread, particularly as the crypto industry experiments with using digital currencies and blockchain networks to enable payments between AI systems.

Qureshi, who spends much of his time looking at the intersection of crypto and AI, said he is particularly interested in “agentic payments”, where AI agents make payments on behalf of users or transact with one another.

“It’s early, but it’s where I see the smartest founders trying out new ideas,” Qureshi said.

Hacks and cybersecurity are also likely to be topics of conversation following a spate of recent attacks, including the US$388 million heist at crypto exchange Bitget just two weeks ago.

Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said that, for her, the value of Token2049 lies less in what happens on stage than in the conversations off it. “It is a useful opportunity to compare what we are seeing at Bitget with what the broader market is prioritising,” she said.

Chen would like to see more regulators and policymakers speaking at the event, particularly as the industry grapples with how stablecoins, tokenised assets and crypto platforms should fit into the wider financial system.

Some of the most consequential questions “cannot be answered by the industry alone”, she said.

Singapore is cementing its status as a major digital-asset hub, with Chainalysis data showing US$284 billion of crypto activity in the city-state between July 2025 and June 2026, up 55.4% from the previous year.

This week it will host hundreds of side events around Token2049.

“Token2049 is one of the key points on the industry calendar,” said conference co-founder Alex Fiskum. “It’s an opportunity to take stock of where the industry stands, build new partnerships and set the agenda for the year ahead.”

title: Google, Constellation near billion-dollar deal for nuclear power
article:
(Oct 6): Google parent Alphabet Inc is close to an agreement to buy nuclear energy from Constellation Energy Corp, as technology companies race to line up power for the data-centre boom.

The tech giant is nearing a deal to pay Constellation US$1 billion or more over the course of a multi-year agreement that’s expected to be announced as soon as this week, according to people familiar with the discussions, who asked not to be named because the information is private.

Constellation, the biggest US reactor operator, and Google declined to comment on Monday. The exact scale and location of the nuclear capacity couldn’t be determined.

The immense amount of electricity required for the artificial intelligence boom is helping to revive interest in nuclear energy, which offers around the clock power that’s also emissions-free. Recent deals have focused on existing facilities as new reactors can take a decade or more to permit and build, and the next wave of fission technology is still likely years from widespread deployment.

Amazon.com Inc struck a similar deal last week with Constellation. The cloud and e-commerce company agreed to buy 690 megawatts of power, including capacity from upgrading the Calvert Cliffs nuclear facility in Maryland.

Google already has multiple agreements with atomic power producers. It agreed last year to buy electricity from NextEra Energy Inc, a deal that will support the power company’s plans to restart its Duane Arnold reactor in Iowa that’s been shuttered since 2020. And last month the tech company lined up new capacity from Southern Co by funding upgrades at two atomic plants.

See also: The only billionaires making money this year are in tech

And Microsoft Corp agreed to buy the electricity from the shuttered Three Mile Island nuclear plant in 2024. Constellation is planning to restart its reactor at the site in Pennsylvania next year.

While safety risks and heavy cost overruns saw the world sour on atomic energy early last decade, it’s been undergoing a global revival over the last few years. As well as surging demand from the tech sector for data centres, nuclear power is being embraced by many nations as a way to cope with a jump in electricity consumption while cutting emissions.

title: Singapore-headquartered data centre operator DayOne files Nasdaq IPO
article:
Singapore-headquartered DayOne Data Centers has filed for a Nasdaq IPO, confirming talks that it will not go ahead with a dual Nasdaq-SGX listing as earlier floated.

For the six months ended June, the data centre operator reported a net loss of US$81.9 million on revenue of US$512 million, compared with a net loss of US$13.5 million on revenue of US$151.5 million in the year earlier period.

According to various reports previously, DayOne is expected to have a market cap of US$20 billion with the IPO.

DayOne is linked to Shanghai-based GDS Holdings, China's largest data centre operator, which runs more than 100 data centres in China.

ST Telemedia, a unit of Temasek Holdings, is known to be an investor of GDS Holding, which was founded by William Huang.

DayOne, previously called GDS International, is a distinct entity that operates data centres outside China in ten markets ranging from Finland to Indonesia. It has secured some 2.3 GW in bookings.

See also: Mi Material Holding Limited files draft prospectus for Mainboard listing

In Singapore, it broke ground last July to build a 20MW data centre at Jurong East. Spanning 40,000 sqm, the first phase of this data centre will be ready for service this year, according to an announcement then.

Lim Ah Doo, previously on the board of EDB Investments and Singapore Technologies Engineering, is DayOne's chairman.

Jamie Khoo, CEO of DayOne since March 2024, spent more than a decade with ST Telemedia before another decade at GDS Holdings.
